questions.q: In a narrative composition, the climax is
o: the point of greatest tension, where the story turns
the opening paragraph that introduces the setting
the list of characters given before the story
the moral stated in the last line
questions.why: The climax is the turning point that the earlier events build towards; the resolution follows it.

questions.q: Which opening is most likely to hook the reader of a narrative?
o: 'This is a story about a day in my life.'
'The phone rang at three in the morning, and I knew before I answered that something was wrong.'
'I am now going to tell you what happened to me.'
'Once there was a day which was a normal day.'
questions.why: It drops the reader into a tense moment and raises a question they want answered.

questions.q: A narrative of something that happened last summer should normally be told in
o: a mix of present and future tenses
the past tense, kept consistent throughout
whichever tense each sentence seems to need
questions.why: Switching tenses without reason confuses the time line; past events are narrated in the past tense.

questions.q: The ICSE English Language paper asks you to write a composition of about
questions.why: Question 1 of Paper 1 sets a 350–400 word composition, so plan a story that fits that length.

questions.q: 'Show, don't tell' advises a writer to
o: reveal feelings through actions, speech and detail instead of naming them
explain every feeling directly to the reader
questions.why: 'Her hands shook as she opened the envelope' shows fear; 'she was afraid' only tells it.

long.q: Write a narrative composition (350–400 words) entitled 'The Day the Lights Went Out in Our Colony'. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: an engaging opening that sets the scene and time of the power cut
B1: a clear sequence of events with a beginning, development and ending
B1: a definite climax or turning point
B1: characters brought alive through action and dialogue
B1: varied sentence structures and lengths used for effect
B1: precise, well-chosen vocabulary suited to the task
B1: clear paragraphing with linked ideas
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar, within 350–400 words

long.q: Give two reasons why dialogue can improve a narrative composition, and write one correctly punctuated line of dialogue as an example.
scheme: B1: it reveals character (how people speak shows who they are)
B1: it moves the action on or adds variety and pace
B1: a line of dialogue with inverted commas, a comma or full stop inside them and a reporting clause, e.g. 'Hurry up,' Amma called from the gate.

long.q: Rewrite this sentence so that it shows rather than tells: 'Ravi was very frightened.' Then explain what your version does.
scheme: B1: a physical reaction is shown (e.g. his knees trembled, his mouth went dry)
B1: a detail of the setting or a sound adds to the fear (e.g. a door creaked in the dark corridor)
B1: explanation: the reader works out the emotion from the details, which is more vivid

long.q: You are to write a story called 'An Unexpected Guest'. Plan it in four stages and state briefly what happens in each.
scheme: B1: opening: characters and setting introduced (e.g. a quiet evening at home in Shimla)
B1: complication: the guest arrives and something puzzling happens
B1: climax: the moment of greatest tension or surprise
B1: resolution: how the situation ends and what the narrator feels or learns

long.q: Write a narrative composition (350–400 words) that begins: 'Nobody believed me when I said the old well behind our school was not empty.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: begins with the given words and follows on from them naturally
B1: builds suspense about what is in the well
B1: a satisfying climax and ending that answer the opening
B1: consistent first-person narration and past tense
B1: varied sentence structures and lengths used for effect
B1: precise, well-chosen vocabulary suited to the task
B1: clear paragraphing with linked ideas
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar, within 350–400 words

questions.q: A descriptive composition mainly aims to
o: tell a story with a twist at the end
create a vivid picture of a person, place or scene
argue for one side of a debate
questions.why: Description builds atmosphere and detail; events matter less than the picture created.

questions.q: Which sentence appeals to the sense of smell?
o: The lane outside the bakery glowed orange in the evening light.
The lane outside the bakery echoed with bicycle bells.
The lane outside the bakery was thick with the scent of warm bread.
The lane outside the bakery was rough and uneven underfoot.
questions.why: 'Scent' is a smell; the others appeal to sight, hearing and touch.

questions.q: What is a sensible way to organise a description of a crowded railway platform?
o: List every object on the platform in alphabetical order
Jump between unrelated places to surprise the reader
Move in a clear order, such as from the entrance to the edge of the track, or from the wide view to small details
questions.why: A spatial or wide-to-close order lets the reader follow the scene as if walking through it.

questions.q: 'The monsoon clouds sulked over Mumbai all afternoon.' The figure of speech used is
questions.why: Sulking is a human mood given to clouds, which is personification.

questions.q: Which habit weakens a descriptive composition most?
o: Repeating vague words such as 'nice' and 'good'
Including sounds and smells as well as sights
questions.why: Vague words give the reader nothing to picture; precise words do the describing.

long.q: Describe a busy vegetable market in your town early on a Sunday morning (350–400 words). (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a clear sense of time (early morning) and place established at the start
B1: details that appeal to at least three senses
B1: a sustained atmosphere rather than a story of events
B1: figurative language (simile, metaphor, personification) used effectively
B1: varied sentence structures and lengths used for effect
B1: precise, well-chosen vocabulary suited to the task
B1: clear paragraphing with linked ideas
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar, within 350–400 words

long.q: Write three sentences describing a temple courtyard at dusk. Each sentence must appeal to a different sense; name the sense in brackets after it.
scheme: B1: first sentence appeals clearly to the named sense (e.g. sight: oil lamps flickering along the steps)
B1: second sentence appeals to a different named sense (e.g. hearing: the clang of the evening bell)
B1: third sentence appeals to a third named sense (e.g. smell: sandalwood and marigold)

long.q: Explain the difference between a descriptive composition and a narrative composition, and give one example of a suitable title for each.
scheme: B1: descriptive writing builds a picture or atmosphere of a person, place or scene
B1: narrative writing tells a sequence of events with a plot
B1: a suitable descriptive title (e.g. 'A Railway Station at Midnight')
B1: a suitable narrative title (e.g. 'The Night I Missed the Last Train')

long.q: Rewrite this sentence, replacing every vague word with precise description: 'It was a nice day and the garden looked good with lots of nice flowers.'
scheme: B1: 'nice day' replaced with specific weather or light (e.g. a crisp, sunlit November morning)
B1: 'looked good' replaced with a precise verb or image
B1: 'lots of nice flowers' replaced with named flowers and colours (e.g. rows of yellow marigolds and crimson roses)

long.q: Describe an elderly person in your neighbourhood whom you admire: their appearance, habits and the effect they have on the people around them (350–400 words). (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a clear physical picture of the person
B1: habits and mannerisms that reveal character
B1: the effect of the person on others shown through examples
B1: a closing reflection on why the writer admires them
B1: varied sentence structures and lengths used for effect
B1: precise, well-chosen vocabulary suited to the task
B1: clear paragraphing with linked ideas
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar, within 350–400 words

questions.q: Which is a suitable way to end an informal letter to your cousin?
questions.why: Informal letters close warmly; 'Yours faithfully' belongs to formal letters.

questions.q: Which of these does an informal letter NOT need?
questions.why: A subject line is part of a formal letter; letters to friends and family leave it out.

questions.q: The tone of an informal letter should be
questions.why: You are writing to someone you know well, so write as you would naturally speak to them.

questions.q: Which is the best opening line for a letter to a friend you have not written to for months?
o: 'I am writing to lodge a complaint about the service.'
'I am sorry I haven't written for so long; the exams kept me busier than ever.'
'With reference to your letter dated 3rd March, I wish to inform you...'
'Kindly grant me leave for two days.'
questions.why: It is friendly, personal and explains the gap; the others are formal-letter openings.

questions.q: Which salutation is correct for a letter to your grandfather?
questions.why: A family letter uses an affectionate, personal salutation.

long.q: Write a letter to your grandmother in Lucknow describing how your family celebrated Diwali this year and inviting her to spend the winter holidays with you. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: writer's address and date at the top
B1: a suitable salutation and an affectionate close with the writer's name
B1: a lively description of the celebrations with specific details
B1: a clear invitation with reasons and practical details
B1: a warm, natural tone suited to a grandparent
B1: well-organised paragraphs: opening, description, invitation, closing
B1: varied, accurate expression
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

long.q: Name, in order, the parts of an informal letter.
scheme: B1: writer's address and the date (top)
B1: salutation (e.g. Dear Aarav,)
B1: body in paragraphs
B1: complimentary close and the writer's name (e.g. Your loving friend, Kavya)

long.q: Your friend scored poorly in a mathematics test and is upset. Write the main paragraph (about 80 words) of a letter giving advice.
scheme: B1: sympathy shown without being dismissive
B1: at least two practical suggestions (e.g. practise daily, ask the teacher about mistakes)
B1: encouragement that one test does not decide everything
B1: friendly tone and accurate language

long.q: State two differences between an informal letter and a formal letter.
scheme: B1: tone and language: friendly and conversational versus polite, precise and impersonal
B1: format: no subject line or receiver's address and a warm close in an informal letter, versus subject line, receiver's address and 'Yours faithfully/sincerely' in a formal one

long.q: Write a letter to a friend who lives in Singapore, persuading him or her to visit Rajasthan with your family during the winter break. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: correct informal format (address, date, salutation, close)
B1: at least two attractions described persuasively (e.g. the forts of Jaipur, the desert at Jaisalmer)
B1: practical details: when, how long, where to stay
B1: persuasive techniques: enthusiasm, answering possible doubts
B1: a friendly, personal tone
B1: logical paragraphs
B1: varied vocabulary
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

topics.name: Letter writing: formal letters and requests

questions.q: A formal letter that begins 'Sir,' or 'Dear Sir/Madam,' usually ends with
questions.why: When the reader is addressed by title rather than name, 'Yours faithfully' is the standard close.

questions.q: The purpose of the subject line in a formal letter is to
o: tell the reader briefly what the letter is about
questions.why: A busy official can see the matter at once, e.g. 'Subject: Request for permission to use the school hall'.

questions.q: Which sentence is suitable for a formal letter?
o: Hey, can we please use the auditorium?
I would be grateful if you could grant us permission to use the auditorium.
You must let us use the auditorium.
Hope you're doing great! Auditorium pls?
questions.why: Formal letters are polite and complete, without slang or demands.

questions.q: Which order of parts is correct for a formal letter?
o: Salutation, subject, date, body, sender's address, close
Subject, body, salutation, receiver's address, date, close
Sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation, body, close, name
Date, close, body, salutation, receiver's address, subject
questions.why: The addresses and date come first, the subject just before the salutation, and the close at the end.

questions.q: The first paragraph of a formal letter should normally
o: give personal news about the family
thank the reader for a gift
state the purpose of the letter clearly
questions.why: Officials want to know at once why you are writing; details follow in the next paragraph.

long.q: Write a letter to the Principal of your school requesting permission to start an Environment Club. Explain what the club would do and how it would benefit the school. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: correct formal format: sender's address, date, receiver's designation and address
B1: a clear, concise subject line
B1: suitable salutation (Sir/Madam) and close (Yours faithfully/obediently) with name and class
B1: purpose stated in the first paragraph
B1: at least two planned activities (e.g. a composting unit, a paper-recycling drive)
B1: benefits to the school explained
B1: polite, formal tone throughout
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

long.q: Write the subject line and the opening paragraph of a letter to the Branch Manager of your bank requesting a new passbook, as yours has been damaged.
scheme: B1: subject line that is brief and specific (e.g. Subject: Request for a duplicate passbook)
B1: opening paragraph states who you are (account holder) and the request
B1: formal, polite tone with no unnecessary detail

long.q: Rewrite these sentences in a formal register: (a) 'Pls fix the fan in our class asap.' (b) 'We want a longer lunch break, it's way too short!'
scheme: B1: (a) polite request form (e.g. I request you to have the fan in our classroom repaired)
B1: (a) abbreviations replaced (e.g. 'at the earliest')
B1: (b) demand turned into a request (e.g. We would be grateful if the lunch break could be extended)
B1: (b) reason given calmly in complete sentences

long.q: Explain why a formal letter should be concise, and give two ways of making it so.
scheme: B1: the reader is busy and must find the main point quickly
B1: keep to one purpose and leave out irrelevant personal details
B1: use short, clear paragraphs and avoid repeating points

long.q: Write a letter to the Director of the Nehru Science Centre requesting permission for your class to visit the centre on a weekday, with a guided tour. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: correct formal layout
B1: clear subject line
B1: the request and the proposed date stated early
B1: practical details: number of students, teachers accompanying, time
B1: the educational purpose of the visit explained
B1: request for confirmation or charges
B1: courteous formal tone and close
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

questions.q: A good notice is
o: brief and clear, and gives all the essential information
long and personal, like a letter
written in verse to attract attention
questions.why: A notice is read quickly on a board, so it must be short and complete.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT usually part of a notice?
o: A complimentary close such as 'Yours faithfully'
The name and designation of the person issuing it
questions.why: A notice has no salutation or letter close; it ends with the issuer's name and designation.

questions.q: In the ICSE English Language paper, a notice must be written in
questions.why: The notice and the email are short tasks with a word limit of 50 words each.

questions.q: Which is the best heading for a notice about a quiz?
questions.why: A heading should say exactly what the notice is about, usually in capitals.

questions.q: Checking 'what, when, where, who and how' before writing a notice makes sure that
o: every essential detail the reader needs is included
the notice is longer than 50 words
the issuer's phone number is hidden
questions.why: Readers must know the event, date and time, venue, who may take part and how to join.

long.q: You are the Secretary of the Literary Club of Green Valley School, Pune. Write a notice (not more than 50 words) informing students of an inter-class debate and inviting names. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: school name, the word NOTICE and the date
B1: a clear heading
B1: what, when and where (topic, date, time, venue)
B1: who may take part and how and by when to give names
B1: issuer's name and designation; within 50 words

long.q: As Head Girl of St. Anne's School, Kochi, write a notice (not more than 50 words) about a blood donation camp being organised in the school for parents and staff. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: school name, NOTICE and date
B1: a precise heading
B1: date, time and venue of the camp
B1: who can donate and any condition (e.g. age 18–60, in good health) or registration detail
B1: issuer's name and designation; within 50 words

long.q: State three features of a good notice.
scheme: B1: brief and within the word limit
B1: a clear heading, date and issuing authority
B1: all essential details (what, when, where, who, how) in simple language

long.q: Identify four faults in this notice and say how you would correct each: 'NOTICE. Dear students, there will be a picnic sometime next month, everybody should come it will be fun. Yours faithfully, Rahul.'
scheme: B1: no name of the school or date of issue; add both at the top
B1: a salutation and letter close are used; remove them
B1: no exact date, time, venue or cost; add these details
B1: no heading or issuer's designation; add e.g. 'CLASS PICNIC' and 'Rahul Mehta, Class Monitor, IX B'

long.q: You are the Secretary of the Residents' Welfare Association, Shanti Apartments, Kolkata. Write a notice (not more than 50 words) informing residents that the water supply will be stopped for a day for tank cleaning. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: name of the association, NOTICE and date
B1: a clear heading (e.g. SUSPENSION OF WATER SUPPLY)
B1: day and hours of the interruption and the reason
B1: advice to residents (e.g. store water in advance)
B1: issuer's name and designation; within 50 words

questions.q: Which field of an email tells the reader what it is about?
questions.why: The subject line, like that of a formal letter, states the topic in a few words.

questions.q: Putting an address in the 'CC' field of an email
o: sends a secret copy that no one else can see
deletes the email after it is read
sends a copy to that person, and all recipients can see they received it
makes that person the main recipient
questions.why: CC is a 'carbon copy' and is visible; BCC (blind carbon copy) is hidden.

questions.q: Which is the best subject line for an email asking the school librarian to extend the return date of a book?
o: Request to extend the return date of a library book
questions.why: It is specific and polite, so the librarian knows the request before opening it.

questions.q: Which opening suits an email to your class teacher?
o: Dear Ms Iyer, I am writing to ask whether I may submit my project on Monday.
questions.why: An email to a teacher follows formal conventions: proper salutation, full sentences, polite request.

questions.q: Why should a formal email avoid abbreviations such as 'pls' and 'u'?
o: They take up too much space
They are too casual and can seem careless or disrespectful
They are not allowed in the English language
questions.why: Formal emails are judged like formal letters; full words show care and respect for the reader.

long.q: Write an email (not more than 50 words) to your class teacher informing her that you will be absent for three days to attend a family wedding in Jaipur, and asking how to catch up on the work missed. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: From, To, Date and a clear Subject line
B1: suitable salutation
B1: the dates and the reason for absence
B1: a polite request about the missed work
B1: suitable close and name; within 50 words

long.q: You ordered a school bag online and it arrived with a broken zip. Write an email (not more than 50 words) to the customer care department asking for a replacement. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: From, To, Date and a specific Subject (with the order number)
B1: formal salutation
B1: the problem stated clearly with the order date
B1: the action requested (replacement or refund) politely but firmly
B1: formal close and name; within 50 words

long.q: Write a suitable subject line for each email: (a) inviting a doctor to speak at your school on healthy eating; (b) informing your coach that you have injured your ankle; (c) asking a bookshop whether a dictionary is in stock.
scheme: B1: (a) e.g. Invitation to speak on healthy eating at our school
B1: (b) e.g. Unable to attend practice owing to an ankle injury
B1: (c) e.g. Enquiry about the availability of a dictionary

long.q: Give two differences between a formal email and a formal letter.
scheme: B1: an email has header fields (From, To, Date, Subject) instead of written addresses
B1: an email is usually shorter and is sent and answered almost at once

long.q: Write an email (not more than 50 words) to the organiser of an inter-school science exhibition registering two students from your school and asking about the size of the display space. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: correct header fields with a clear subject
B1: formal salutation
B1: names and class of the two students and the project title
B1: the question about display space asked clearly
B1: formal close with name and designation; within 50 words

questions.q: Read: 'Although the train was two hours late, Meera did not complain; she opened her book and was soon lost in another world.' What does this tell us about Meera?
o: She is angry about the delay
She has never travelled by train
She is patient and enjoys reading
questions.why: 'Did not complain' shows patience and 'lost in another world' shows how absorbed she is in her book.

questions.q: When asked to 'give the meaning of a word as used in the passage', you should
o: copy the sentence the word appears in
give every meaning listed in a dictionary
give the meaning that fits that word's context in the sentence
questions.why: Many words have several meanings; only the one that fits the passage earns the mark.

questions.q: Read: 'The village well had dried up long ago, so every morning the women walked three kilometres to the river.' Why did the women walk to the river?
o: Because the village well had dried up
Because they enjoyed the morning walk
Because the river water was cleaner
Because the well was three kilometres away
questions.why: The word 'so' links the cause (the dry well) to the result (the walk).

questions.q: What is the best first step with an unseen passage?
o: Answer the summary question first without reading
Read the whole passage once for its general sense before looking at the questions in detail
questions.why: A first reading gives the overall meaning, which makes the detailed answers more accurate.

questions.q: Read: 'Kabir's grandfather mended watches in a shop no bigger than a cupboard, yet people came from three towns away.' What does 'yet' suggest?
o: The shop was too small for customers
Despite the tiny shop, his skill was widely respected
His shop was in three towns
questions.why: 'Yet' sets up a contrast: the shop is small but his reputation is large.

long.q: Read the passage and answer the questions. 'On the morning of Uttarayan, Dhruv climbed onto the terrace of his building in Ahmedabad before the sun was up. All around him, rooftops were already crowded with families. His father handed him the spool, but Dhruv's fingers were stiff with cold, and his first kite dipped and fell into the neighbour's water tank. Instead of laughing, old Mr Desai next door fished it out, dried it with his towel and showed Dhruv how to hold the string loosely.' (a) Why did Dhruv's first kite fall? (b) How did Mr Desai help him? (c) What does Mr Desai's behaviour suggest about him? (d) Find a word that shows how early Dhruv woke.
scheme: B1: (a) his fingers were stiff with cold, so he could not control it
B1: (b) he took the kite out of the tank, dried it and showed Dhruv how to hold the string loosely
B1: (c) he is kind and patient (he helps rather than mocks)
B1: (d) 'before the sun was up' (or 'already')

long.q: Read: 'The lake had shrunk to a cracked plate of mud. Fishermen sat beside their idle boats, mending nets that had nothing to catch.' Give the meaning of each word as used here: (a) shrunk (b) idle (c) mending.
scheme: B1: (a) shrunk: become much smaller
B1: (b) idle: not being used, not working
B1: (c) mending: repairing

long.q: Read: 'Every evening after school, Tara laced up her old canvas shoes and ran the length of Marine Drive. Her mother worried about the traffic, her friends teased her about her red face, but in six months she had not missed a single day.' In your own words, (a) what did Tara do each evening; (b) what two things might have discouraged her; (c) what quality does the last sentence show?
scheme: B1: (a) she went running along the seafront road after school
B1: (b) her mother's worry about traffic and her friends' teasing
B1: (c) determination or perseverance

long.q: Read: 'The new teacher did not shout. She waited, chalk in hand, until the last whisper died away, and then she smiled.' Quote the phrase that shows the class became silent, and explain what the teacher's method suggests about her.
scheme: B1: 'until the last whisper died away'
B1: she is calm and confident; she controls the class through patience rather than anger

long.q: Read: 'For forty years the banyan tree had shaded the bus stop. When the road was widened, the council marked it for cutting. That night, the shopkeepers of the market tied rakhis round its trunk, and by morning a hundred people were standing beneath it.' (a) Why was the tree to be cut? (b) What did the shopkeepers do? (c) Why do you think they did this? (d) What does the gathering of a hundred people show?
scheme: B1: (a) the road was being widened
B1: (b) they tied rakhis round its trunk
B1: (c) to show they would protect it as a brother or sister is protected (they valued it)
B1: (d) the community cared about the tree and was willing to protest peacefully to save it

questions.q: 'Anjali was meticulous: she checked every sum twice and ruled every margin.' 'Meticulous' means
questions.why: Checking twice and ruling margins are examples of great care with detail.

questions.q: Choose the antonym of 'scarce' in: 'Water is scarce in the desert in May.'
questions.why: 'Scarce' means in short supply; its opposite is 'plentiful'. 'Rare' is a synonym.

questions.q: A person who can speak two languages fluently is
questions.why: 'Bi' means two and 'lingual' refers to language; the others concern two sides or two years.

questions.q: Choose the correct word: 'The ___ of the story is that honesty pays.'
questions.why: 'Moral' is the lesson; 'morale' is confidence or spirit, as in 'the team's morale'.

questions.q: 'Before the board exams, Arjun burnt the midnight oil.' This means he
questions.why: The idiom refers to working late, once done by the light of an oil lamp.

long.q: Give one word for each: (a) a place where bees are kept; (b) a person who cannot be corrected or reformed; (c) a speech made without preparation.
scheme: B1: (a) apiary
B1: (b) incorrigible
B1: (c) extempore (or impromptu)

long.q: Use each word correctly in a sentence of your own: (a) principal, (b) principle, (c) stationary, (d) stationery.
scheme: B1: (a) principal as head of a school or as 'main' (e.g. The principal addressed the assembly.)
B1: (b) principle as a rule or belief (e.g. Honesty is a principle she lives by.)
B1: (c) stationary as not moving (e.g. The bus was stationary at the signal.)
B1: (d) stationery as writing materials (e.g. I bought stationery for the new term.)

long.q: Give the meaning of 'a bolt from the blue' and 'to turn over a new leaf', and use one of them in a sentence.
scheme: B1: a bolt from the blue: a sudden, unexpected event (usually unwelcome)
B1: to turn over a new leaf: to change one's behaviour for the better
B1: a sentence using one idiom correctly

long.q: Give the antonym of the word in capitals that fits each sentence: (a) He was GENEROUS with his time. (b) The fort is an ANCIENT building. (c) Metals EXPAND when heated.
scheme: B1: (a) mean / stingy
B1: (b) modern
B1: (c) contract

long.q: Choose the correct word in each and give a reason: (a) A judge must be (disinterested / uninterested). (b) The loud music did not (affect / effect) his concentration. (c) There were (fewer / less) students than chairs.
scheme: B1: (a) disinterested: it means impartial, not bored
B1: (b) affect: the verb meaning 'to influence'
B1: (c) fewer: used with nouns that can be counted

questions.q: Neither the teacher nor the students ___ aware of the change in the timetable.
questions.why: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'students', which is plural.

questions.q: By the time we reached the station, the train ___.
questions.why: The past perfect shows that the leaving happened before another past action (reaching).

questions.q: Each of the boys ___ given a certificate.
questions.why: 'Each' is singular, so it takes a singular verb, whatever noun follows 'of'.

questions.q: She ___ in Chennai since 2019.
questions.why: 'Since' with a point in time that continues to now needs the present perfect.

questions.q: The news from the hospital ___ encouraging today.
questions.why: 'News' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb, and 'today' needs the present.

long.q: Fill in each blank with the correct form of the verb in brackets: 'Last Sunday my father (wake) ___ us at five. We (plan) ___ the trip for weeks. By the time we (reach) ___ the lake, the sun (rise) ___ above the hills.'
scheme: B1: woke
B1: had planned / had been planning
B1: reached
B1: had risen
long.ans: woke; had planned; reached; had risen

long.q: Correct the error in each sentence: (a) One of my friends live in Delhi. (b) Bread and butter are my usual breakfast. (c) Mathematics are my favourite subject.
scheme: B1: (a) One of my friends lives in Delhi. ('one' is the subject)
B1: (b) Bread and butter is my usual breakfast. (a single dish)
B1: (c) Mathematics is my favourite subject.

long.q: Explain the difference in meaning between 'I have finished my project' and 'I finished my project yesterday'.
scheme: B1: the present perfect links the past action to now: the project is done and that matters at present, no time given
B1: the simple past places the action at a finished past time, stated by 'yesterday'

long.q: Fill in the blanks with the correct form of the verb in brackets: (a) The Ganga (flow) ___ from the Himalayas to the Bay of Bengal. (b) Look! The children (play) ___ cricket in the rain. (c) If it rains tomorrow, we (stay) ___ indoors. (d) She (wait) ___ for an hour when the bus finally came.
scheme: B1: (a) flows (a general fact)
B1: (b) are playing (happening now)
B1: (c) will stay (first conditional)
B1: (d) had been waiting
long.ans: (a) flows (b) are playing (c) will stay (d) had been waiting

long.q: Rewrite in the past tense: 'Priya opens the gate, walks to the door and finds that someone has left a parcel.'
scheme: B1: opened
B1: walked, found
B1: had left (the earlier action moves to the past perfect)
long.ans: Priya opened the gate, walked to the door and found that someone had left a parcel.

questions.q: She is fond ___ classical music.
questions.why: 'Fond' is always followed by 'of'.

questions.q: The meeting was put ___ because the chief guest was unwell.
questions.why: 'Put off' means postpone; 'put out' means extinguish.

questions.q: He has been ill ___ Monday.
questions.why: 'Since' is used with a point in time; 'for' is used with a length of time, e.g. 'for three days'.

questions.q: Please look ___ my dog while I am in Bengaluru.
questions.why: 'Look after' means take care of; 'look into' means investigate.

questions.q: The thieves broke ___ the shop through the back window.
questions.why: 'Break into' means to enter by force; 'break down' means to stop working.

long.q: Fill in the blanks with suitable prepositions: (a) The cat jumped ___ the wall. (b) I have lived in Nagpur ___ ten years. (c) He was accused ___ theft. (d) Divide the sweets ___ the four children.
scheme: B1: (a) over / onto
B1: (b) for
B1: (c) of
B1: (d) among

long.q: Give the meaning of each phrasal verb and use it in a sentence: (a) give up (b) carry out (c) look into.
scheme: B1: (a) give up: stop doing or trying, with a correct sentence
B1: (b) carry out: perform or complete (a task or order), with a correct sentence
B1: (c) look into: investigate, with a correct sentence

long.q: Replace the words in capitals with a suitable phrasal verb: (a) The firemen EXTINGUISHED the blaze. (b) I cannot TOLERATE his rudeness. (c) The police will INVESTIGATE the matter. (d) The plane DEPARTED on time.
scheme: B1: (a) put out
B1: (b) put up with
B1: (c) look into
B1: (d) took off
long.ans: (a) put out (b) put up with (c) look into (d) took off

long.q: Correct the use of prepositions: (a) He is senior than me. (b) She is married with a doctor. (c) Let us discuss about the plan.
scheme: B1: (a) He is senior to me.
B1: (b) She is married to a doctor.
B1: (c) Let us discuss the plan. ('discuss' takes no preposition)
long.ans: (a) senior to (b) married to (c) discuss the plan

long.q: Explain the difference between 'in' and 'into', and between 'between' and 'among', with an example sentence for each.
scheme: B1: 'in' shows position inside; 'into' shows movement towards the inside
B1: examples, e.g. The fish are in the pond. / The boy dived into the pond.
B1: 'between' is generally used for two; 'among' for more than two
B1: examples, e.g. between the two schools / among the five friends

questions.q: An argumentative composition must
o: tell a story with a surprise ending
describe a place in detail without giving an opinion
take a clear position and support it with reasons and examples
questions.why: The examiner looks for a definite stand, developed logically and backed with evidence.

questions.q: Why should you mention and answer the opposing view in an argumentative composition?
o: It fills up the word count
It shows that you have no opinion of your own
The examiner requires you to agree with both sides
Answering a counter-argument shows you have weighed both sides and makes your case stronger
questions.why: Rebutting an objection persuades the reader that your view holds up under challenge.

questions.q: Which is the strongest topic sentence for a paragraph supporting homework?
o: Homework, when it is set sensibly, builds the habit of independent study that board exams demand.
Homework is a thing that exists.
Some people like homework and some do not.
I am going to talk about homework now.
questions.why: It makes a clear, specific claim that the rest of the paragraph can prove.

questions.q: Which connective introduces a contrasting point?
questions.why: 'However' signals a turn to the other side; the others add a similar point.

questions.q: Which is the weakest support for an argument?
o: A statistic from a government survey
A specific example from your own city
A quotation from an expert in the field
questions.why: An appeal to 'everybody' gives no evidence; facts, examples and expert views do.

long.q: 'Mobile phones should be banned in schools.' Express your views either for or against this statement (350–400 words). (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a clear stand stated in the introduction
B1: at least three distinct, developed arguments
B1: relevant examples or evidence for each argument
B1: an opposing view acknowledged and answered
B1: varied sentence structures and lengths used for effect
B1: precise, well-chosen vocabulary suited to the task
B1: clear paragraphing with linked ideas
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar, within 350–400 words

long.q: Write a paragraph (about 100 words) rebutting the claim: 'Online classes are just as good as classroom teaching.'
scheme: B1: the claim restated fairly
B1: one strong counter-point (e.g. lack of face-to-face interaction or practical work)
B1: a second point or an example (e.g. unequal internet access in rural areas)
B1: a concluding sentence that reinforces the writer's view

long.q: Give three arguments for the view 'Public transport should be free for school students in Indian cities' and one argument against it.
scheme: B1: for: it reduces traffic and pollution from private vehicles taking children to school
B1: for: it eases the burden on families with low incomes
B1: for: it builds the habit of using public transport
B1: against: the cost to the government or transport corporation, which may lead to poorer services

long.q: Explain two ways in which the conclusion of an argumentative composition differs from a simple summary of the points made.
scheme: B1: it restates the writer's stand firmly, showing that the argument has been proved
B1: it ends with a forceful final thought, such as a call to action or a look to the future, rather than only repeating points

long.q: 'Competitive examinations do more harm than good.' Express your views for or against this statement (350–400 words). (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a clear stand stated early
B1: arguments developed in separate paragraphs
B1: specific examples from the Indian context (e.g. coaching culture, entrance tests)
B1: a counter-argument answered
B1: varied sentence structures and lengths used for effect
B1: precise, well-chosen vocabulary suited to the task
B1: clear paragraphing with linked ideas
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar, within 350–400 words

topics.name: Composition: short story and picture composition

questions.q: In the picture composition, the most important rule is that
o: every object in the picture must be listed
you must describe the picture without any story
the composition must have the same title as the picture
there must be a clear connection between the picture and your composition
questions.why: You may write a story, description or account suggested by the picture, but it must clearly link to it.

questions.q: If a short story must end with given words, you should
o: plan the story so that it leads naturally to those exact words
add the words after an unrelated story
change the words to suit your story
begin the story with those words
questions.why: The ending must grow out of the plot; tacking it on loses marks for relevance.

questions.q: An effective twist ending is one that
o: appears from nowhere with no link to the story
surprises the reader but is prepared for by earlier clues
explains that it was all a dream with no hint
questions.why: A fair twist makes the reader look back and see the clues they missed.

questions.q: Why should a 350–400 word story have only a few characters?
o: Because names take up too many words
So that each one can be developed properly in the space
questions.why: Two or three well-drawn characters work better than many flat ones in a short story.

questions.q: A story narrated using 'he', 'she' and 'they' throughout is told
questions.why: First-person narration uses 'I'; third-person narration stands outside the characters.

long.q: Imagine a picture that shows an elderly man seated under a banyan tree, teaching a group of village children who sit on mats with slates; a bicycle leans against the trunk. Write a story, description or account (350–400 words) that the picture suggests to you. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a clear and sustained connection with the picture
B1: an original idea rather than a mere list of what is seen
B1: setting and characters developed
B1: a definite shape: opening, development, ending
B1: varied sentence structures and lengths used for effect
B1: precise, well-chosen vocabulary suited to the task
B1: clear paragraphing with linked ideas
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar, within 350–400 words

long.q: Write a short story (350–400 words) that ends with the words: '...and that was the last time I ever doubted my little sister.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: ends with the exact given words, which follow naturally
B1: the sister's role is central to the plot
B1: the narrator's doubt is established early
B1: a convincing climax
B1: varied sentence structures and lengths used for effect
B1: precise, well-chosen vocabulary suited to the task
B1: clear paragraphing with linked ideas
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar, within 350–400 words

long.q: Give two ways of making a clear connection between a picture and your composition.
scheme: B1: build the story around the main figure or event shown in the picture
B1: include an important detail from the picture as a turning point or refer to it in the opening and ending

long.q: Write the opening paragraph (about 80 words) of a story called 'The Wrong Bus'.
scheme: B1: setting established (place and time)
B1: the main character introduced
B1: the problem (boarding the wrong bus) hinted at or revealed
B1: a hook that makes the reader want to go on

long.q: Explain what foreshadowing is, and give an example of a sentence that could foreshadow a later event in a story.
scheme: B1: foreshadowing is a hint early in the story of what will happen later
B1: it builds suspense and makes the ending feel prepared for
B1: a suitable example (e.g. 'Nobody noticed the dark clouds gathering behind the hill as we set off.')

topics.name: Letter writing: complaints and letters to the editor

questions.q: A letter to the editor of a newspaper usually aims to
o: draw public attention to an issue of general concern
ask the editor for a personal favour
questions.why: Such letters are written for publication, so they deal with matters affecting the public.

questions.q: Which detail is most important in a letter of complaint about a faulty product?
o: Specific facts such as the date of purchase, the order number and the exact fault
A long story about the writer's day
questions.why: Precise details let the company act; vague anger does not.

questions.q: The tone of a complaint letter should be
questions.why: You want action, so you state the problem clearly and courteously.

questions.q: Which sentence clearly requests action?
o: I request you to replace the defective heater within a week.
questions.why: A complaint should end by asking for a specific remedy and a time frame.

questions.q: Which salutation is suitable for a letter to the editor?
questions.why: Letters to the editor use a formal salutation such as 'Sir,' or 'Dear Sir/Madam,'.

long.q: Write a letter to the editor of a national daily about the disturbance caused by loudspeakers being played late at night in your locality, and suggest what should be done. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: correct formal layout with the editor's address
B1: a precise subject line
B1: request to publish or to draw the authorities' attention, in the opening
B1: the problem described with specific effects (students, the sick, the elderly)
B1: at least two practical suggestions (e.g. enforce time limits, fix volume levels)
B1: a formal, reasoned tone
B1: well-organised paragraphs
B1: accurate spelling, punctuation and grammar

long.q: You bought a mixer-grinder online and it stopped working within a week. Write a letter of complaint to the Customer Service Manager of the company. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: correct formal format
B1: subject line including the order number
B1: purchase details (date, model, order number)
B1: the fault described precisely
B1: the remedy asked for (repair, replacement or refund) with a time frame
B1: firm but polite tone
B1: logical paragraphs
B1: accurate language

long.q: Write a suitable subject line for a letter to the editor about waterlogging in your locality during the monsoon, and explain why it is effective.
scheme: B1: a concise, specific subject (e.g. Severe waterlogging in Sector 12 during the monsoon)
B1: explanation: it names the problem and place so the editor and readers see the issue at once

long.q: Rewrite this sentence so that it suits a formal complaint: 'Your company is useless and I want my money back right now.'
scheme: B1: the insult removed and the problem stated factually
B1: a polite but firm request, e.g. 'As the product does not work, I request a full refund within seven days.'

long.q: State four points you would include in a letter to the Municipal Commissioner complaining about irregular garbage collection in your area.
scheme: B1: the area affected and how long the problem has lasted
B1: the effects: smell, flies, stray animals, risk of disease
B1: earlier complaints made with no result
B1: the action requested (e.g. a daily collection schedule, more bins)

questions.q: In the ICSE paper, the email task is usually
o: on a topic unrelated to the notice
linked to the notice, for example written to someone connected with the event in the notice
questions.why: The two 50-word tasks normally share one situation, so plan the details once and use them in both.

questions.q: Which sentence is in the passive style often used in notices?
o: I want all of you to come to the hall.
Students are requested to assemble in the hall at 9 a.m.
We had a great time in the hall.
questions.why: Notices are impersonal; the passive 'are requested' keeps the tone formal and brief.

questions.q: Which details are essential in a notice for a charity fair?
o: A long history of the school
A list of every visitor last year
Date, time, venue and the purpose of the fair
questions.why: Without these, readers cannot attend or understand why the fair is being held.

questions.q: An email inviting a guest speaker should include
o: the date, time and topic, and a polite request to confirm
questions.why: The speaker needs all the practical details and should know a reply is expected.

questions.q: Which 'From' address is most suitable for a formal email sent on behalf of a school club?
questions.why: A formal email should come from a sensible address that identifies the sender.

long.q: You are the Sports Captain of Holy Cross School, Bhopal. Write a notice (not more than 50 words) asking for volunteers to help organise the Annual Sports Day. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: school name, NOTICE and date
B1: a clear heading
B1: the event's date and the jobs volunteers will do
B1: who may apply, how and by when
B1: issuer's name and designation; within 50 words

long.q: Write an email (not more than 50 words) to the district athletics coach inviting her to be the guest of honour at the Annual Sports Day. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: correct header fields with a clear subject
B1: formal salutation
B1: date, time and venue of the event
B1: the role requested and a request to confirm
B1: formal close with name and designation; within 50 words

long.q: As Secretary of the Residents' Welfare Association, Lake View Colony, Bhubaneswar, write a notice (not more than 50 words) about a tree-plantation drive. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: association name, NOTICE and date
B1: a suitable heading
B1: date, time and meeting point
B1: what residents should bring or do
B1: issuer's name and designation; within 50 words

long.q: Write an email (not more than 50 words) to the Horticulture Department of the Municipal Corporation requesting 100 saplings for the plantation drive. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: header fields with a specific subject
B1: formal salutation
B1: the request with number of saplings, and kinds if possible
B1: date needed and delivery or collection details
B1: formal close and designation; within 50 words

long.q: Point out two faults in this email and rewrite its subject line and first sentence correctly. 'Subject: hi. hey sir, we r having a quiz n u should come.'
scheme: B1: the subject line does not state the purpose
B1: the language is informal (abbreviations, 'hey', no capital letters)
B1: improved subject, e.g. Invitation to judge the Inter-School Quiz
B1: improved opening, e.g. 'Dear Sir, We would be honoured if you could judge our Inter-School Quiz on 12th December.'

topics.name: Comprehension: inference and the writer's craft

questions.q: Read: 'The house had been empty for years; the gate hung by one hinge and the windows stared at the street like blind eyes.' The simile suggests the house is
questions.why: Blind, staring eyes suggest emptiness and neglect, matching the broken gate.

questions.q: A question asking 'What does the writer imply...?' wants you to
o: copy a sentence from the passage
count the words in the paragraph
work out a meaning that is suggested but not stated
questions.why: An implication is read between the lines, using clues in the text as evidence.

questions.q: Read: 'Grandmother never threw anything away. Rubber bands lived on the door handle, string in a tin, and every plastic bag was folded into a neat triangle.' The writer mainly shows that Grandmother is
questions.why: Saving and neatly folding everything shows thrift and orderliness.

questions.q: Read: 'Crash! The pile of steel plates slid from the shelf.' The word 'Crash!' is an example of
questions.why: The word imitates the sound it describes.

questions.q: Why might a writer use a very short sentence after several long ones?
o: To make the passage harder to read
Because short sentences are always wrong
To create sudden emphasis or tension
questions.why: A short sentence stands out against long ones, so it highlights a key moment.

long.q: Read: 'Sunita stood at the edge of the stage, the certificate trembling in her hand. Out there, somewhere in the dark rows, sat the teacher who had told her she would never be a speaker. She took a breath, stepped into the light, and began.' (a) Why was the certificate trembling? (b) Why is the teacher mentioned at this moment? (c) What does 'stepped into the light' suggest, besides its literal meaning?
scheme: B1: (a) her hand was shaking with nervousness
B1: (b) to show her nerves come partly from that teacher's doubt and that this is a chance to prove him or her wrong
B1: (c) it suggests courage or coming out of fear and doubt into confidence and success

long.q: Read: 'The river was a thief. Each monsoon it crept a little closer, taking a field here, a cowshed there, until the Sharmas' house stood alone on a shrinking island of earth.' (a) Explain the metaphor in the first sentence. (b) What does 'crept' suggest about the river? (c) What is the writer's purpose in this passage?
scheme: B1: (a) the river is called a thief because it steals land from people
B1: (b) it moves slowly and secretly, so people hardly notice the danger
B1: (c) to show the gradual threat of erosion and the family's helplessness or isolation

long.q: Read: 'At the interview, Mr Rao asked only one question. He did not look at Kiran's certificates. He looked at her shoes, which she had polished at midnight, and smiled.' What does the writer imply about (a) Kiran and (b) Mr Rao? Give evidence for each.
scheme: B1: (a) Kiran is careful and serious about the job; she polished her shoes at midnight
B1: (b) Mr Rao values character and effort more than paper qualifications; he ignores the certificates and smiles at the shoes

long.q: Read: 'The city never sleeps, people say. But at four in the morning, on the empty flyover, I heard it breathing.' (a) Identify the figure of speech in the last clause. (b) What mood does the passage create? (c) How does the word 'But' change the direction of the passage?
scheme: B1: (a) personification: the city is said to breathe
B1: (b) a calm, quiet, slightly mysterious mood
B1: (c) it contrasts the common saying with what the narrator actually experienced

long.q: Read: 'Every year the school magazine praised the toppers. This year, on the last page, there was a small photograph of Ramu, the gardener, who had retired after thirty years. Beneath it someone had written: "He grew everything here, including us."' (a) Why is the photograph's position significant? (b) Explain the caption. (c) What is the writer suggesting about how we value people? (d) Comment on the effect of the word 'small'.
scheme: B1: (a) the last page shows he is usually overlooked compared with the toppers
B1: (b) he grew the plants and, through his care, helped the students grow up
B1: (c) quiet workers who support everyone deserve as much recognition as high achievers
B1: (d) 'small' stresses how modest the tribute is compared with his long service

questions.q: A good summary is written
o: by copying the most important sentences
in your own words, giving only the main points
questions.why: Summarising tests whether you can pick out the key points and express them concisely.

questions.q: Which of these should you leave out of a summary?
questions.why: These support the main ideas but are not themselves the points the question asks for.

questions.q: If a summary question sets a word limit, you should
o: write twice as much to be safe
stay within the limit while covering every relevant point
questions.why: Going over the limit can cost marks, and so can missing points.

questions.q: The first step in writing a summary is to
o: count the words in the passage
mark the points in the passage that answer the question
questions.why: Summaries usually focus on one aspect, so find the relevant points before writing.

questions.q: A summary should be presented as
o: one continuous paragraph of complete sentences
questions.why: ICSE summaries are written as a single paragraph, linking the points smoothly.

long.q: Read the passage and, in not more than 50 words, summarise the benefits of the school's kitchen garden. 'When St. Joseph's School in Mangaluru turned its unused backyard into a kitchen garden, nobody expected much. Within a year, the canteen was serving vegetables grown by the students. Children who had never touched soil learnt how seeds sprout and how much water a tomato plant needs. The science teacher used the garden for lessons on photosynthesis. Shy students found that working together on a vegetable bed was easier than talking in class. And the canteen's bills fell by nearly a quarter.'
scheme: B1: the canteen serves vegetables the students grow
B1: students learn practical gardening
B1: the garden is used for science lessons
B1: shy students mix more easily
B1: the canteen's costs fell by about a quarter
B1: in own words, one paragraph, within 50 words

long.q: Read the passage and summarise, in not more than 40 words, why the narrator's grandfather refused to sell his land. 'The builders offered my grandfather three times what the land was worth. He listened politely and said no. His father had planted the mango trees on it, he explained; the village children played cricket in its clearing every evening; and the well on its edge was the only one that did not dry up in May. Money, he said, would be spent in a year. The land would feed us for ever.'
scheme: B1: the trees were planted by his father (family history)
B1: the village children use it to play
B1: its well provides water when others dry up
B1: land lasts while money is soon spent
B1: own words and within the limit

long.q: Explain why copying sentences from the passage is likely to lose marks in a summary.
scheme: B1: the task tests understanding, which copying does not show
B1: copied sentences include unnecessary detail, so the summary goes over the limit or misses points

long.q: Read: 'Plastic bags are cheap and light, which is precisely the problem. Because they cost almost nothing, people use them once and throw them away. Because they are light, the wind carries them into drains, rivers and the sea, where they choke drains, cause flooding in cities like Mumbai and are swallowed by cows and turtles.' In not more than 30 words, summarise the problems caused by plastic bags.
scheme: B1: they are used once and thrown away because they are cheap
B1: being light, they are blown into drains, rivers and the sea
B1: they block drains, causing flooding
B1: animals swallow them

long.q: Read the passage and, in not more than 50 words, summarise what the writer learnt from the trek. 'I had imagined the trek to Hampta Pass would be about the view. It was, partly. But mostly it was about my feet, which ached, and my lungs, which complained above three thousand metres. I learnt to walk slowly, because those who rushed had to stop more often. I learnt to share my chocolate with the porter, who had carried far more than I had and never complained. And I learnt that the best view of all came after the hardest climb.'
scheme: B1: the trek tested the body, not only the eyes
B1: going slowly is better than rushing
B1: sharing and respect for the hard-working porter
B1: rewards come after the greatest effort
B1: own words, one paragraph, within 50 words

questions.q: Join without using 'and', 'but' or 'so': 'He was tired. He continued working.'
o: Though he was tired, he continued working.
He was tired because he continued working.
Unless he was tired, he continued working.
questions.why: 'Though' shows contrast between tiredness and continuing to work, keeping the original meaning.

questions.q: Join using a relative pronoun: 'This is the boy. He won the chess tournament.'
o: This is the boy which won the chess tournament.
This is the boy who won the chess tournament.
This is the boy whom won the chess tournament.
This is the boy whose won the chess tournament.
questions.why: 'Who' is the subject form used for people.

questions.q: Join to show purpose: 'She worked hard. She wanted to pass the examination.'
o: She worked hard although she passed the examination.
She worked hard unless she passed the examination.
She worked hard so that she could pass the examination.
She worked hard because of passing the examination.
questions.why: 'So that' introduces purpose; the others alter the meaning.

questions.q: Join using 'in spite of': 'Ravi ran fast. He missed the bus.'
o: In spite of he ran fast, Ravi missed the bus.
In spite of Ravi missed the bus, he ran fast.
In spite of to run fast, Ravi missed the bus.
In spite of running fast, Ravi missed the bus.
questions.why: 'In spite of' is followed by a noun or an -ing form, not a full clause.

questions.q: Join using 'no sooner': 'The rain stopped. We went out to play.'
o: No sooner had the rain stopped than we went out to play.
No sooner the rain stopped when we went out to play.
No sooner did the rain stopped than we went out to play.
No sooner had the rain stopped when we went out to play.
questions.why: The pattern is 'No sooner had + past participle ... than ...'.

long.q: Join each pair into one sentence without using 'and', 'but' or 'so': (a) The shop was closed. We returned home. (b) My uncle lives in Ooty. He grows tea. (c) He was ill. He attended the meeting. (d) You must hurry. You will miss the train.
scheme: B1: (a) As the shop was closed, we returned home.
B1: (b) My uncle, who lives in Ooty, grows tea.
B1: (c) Although he was ill, he attended the meeting.
B1: (d) Unless you hurry, you will miss the train. (or: You must hurry or you will miss the train.)

long.q: Join using the word given: (a) I met a man. His son is a pilot. (whose) (b) She is very poor. She cannot buy books. (too) (c) The guests arrived. The host welcomed them. (on)
scheme: B1: (a) I met a man whose son is a pilot.
B1: (b) She is too poor to buy books.
B1: (c) On the guests' arrival, the host welcomed them. (or: On arriving, the guests were welcomed by the host.)
long.ans: (a) whose son is a pilot (b) too poor to buy books (c) On the guests' arrival, the host welcomed them.

long.q: Join into one sentence using a participle: 'She opened the letter. She read it aloud.'
scheme: B1: Opening the letter, she read it aloud. (or: Having opened the letter, she read it aloud.)
B1: the participle phrase refers correctly to 'she' (no dangling participle)

long.q: Join using 'not only...but also': 'He plays the tabla. He sings classical music.'
scheme: B1: He not only plays the tabla but also sings classical music.
B1: the two parts are parallel (verb after 'not only' and verb after 'but also')

long.q: Join each pair using the word in brackets: (a) The train was late. We waited on the platform. (since) (b) He is clever. He is lazy. (although) (c) She did not study. She failed. (if...not, beginning 'If')
scheme: B1: (a) Since the train was late, we waited on the platform.
B1: (b) Although he is clever, he is lazy.
B1: (c) If she had studied, she would not have failed.
long.ans: (a) Since the train was late... (b) Although he is clever, he is lazy. (c) If she had studied, she would not have failed.

questions.q: Rewrite using 'so...that': 'He is too weak to walk.'
o: He is so weak that he can walk.
He is so weak that he cannot walk.
He is weak so that he walks.
He is so weak to walk.
questions.why: 'Too...to' carries a negative meaning, so the 'so...that' version needs 'cannot'.

questions.q: Which sentence means the same as 'No sooner did the bell ring than the students rushed out'?
o: The students rushed out before the bell rang.
The bell rang after the students rushed out.
As soon as the bell rang, the students rushed out.
The bell did not ring, so the students rushed out.
questions.why: 'No sooner...than' and 'as soon as' both show one action immediately following another.

questions.q: Rewrite using 'if': 'Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.'
o: If you hurry, you will miss the bus.
If you do not hurry, you will not miss the bus.
If you hurried, you will miss the bus.
If you do not hurry, you will miss the bus.
questions.why: 'Unless' means 'if...not'.

questions.q: Which sentence keeps the meaning of 'Mount Everest is the highest peak in the world'?
o: No other peak in the world is as high as Mount Everest.
Mount Everest is higher than the highest peak in the world.
Some peaks are higher than Mount Everest.
No other peak in the world is higher than some peaks.
questions.why: A superlative becomes 'No other...as...as' in the positive degree.

questions.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: Hardly he had arrived than it began to rain.
Hardly had he arrived when it began to rain.
Hardly had he arrived than it began to rain.
Hardly did he arrived when it began to rain.
questions.why: 'Hardly' is followed by inverted word order (had he) and pairs with 'when', not 'than'.

long.q: Rewrite each sentence as instructed, without changing the meaning: (a) As soon as she saw the snake, she screamed. (Begin: No sooner...) (b) He is so short that he cannot reach the shelf. (Use: too) (c) It is a pity that you missed the show. (Begin: What a...) (d) If you do not apologise, you will be punished. (Use: unless)
scheme: B1: (a) No sooner did she see the snake than she screamed.
B1: (b) He is too short to reach the shelf.
B1: (c) What a pity that you missed the show!
B1: (d) Unless you apologise, you will be punished.

long.q: Rewrite as instructed: (a) Delhi is larger than any other city in the region. (Use: largest) (b) He was so tired that he could not stand. (Begin: Such...) (c) Although he is rich, he is unhappy. (Use: despite)
scheme: B1: (a) Delhi is the largest city in the region.
B1: (b) Such was his tiredness that he could not stand.
B1: (c) Despite being rich, he is unhappy. (or: Despite his wealth, he is unhappy.)
long.ans: (a) the largest city in the region (b) Such was his tiredness that... (c) Despite being rich, he is unhappy.

long.q: Rewrite as instructed: (a) Nobody could solve the puzzle. (Begin: The puzzle...) (b) I prefer tea to coffee. (Use: rather) (c) She started learning the veena five years ago. (Begin: She has...)
scheme: B1: (a) The puzzle could not be solved by anybody.
B1: (b) I would rather have tea than coffee.
B1: (c) She has been learning the veena for five years.
long.ans: (a) The puzzle could not be solved by anybody. (b) I would rather have tea than coffee. (c) She has been learning the veena for five years.

long.q: Rewrite as instructed: (a) He is the best singer in the class. (Begin: No other...) (b) The moment the guests left, we cleaned up. (Begin: Hardly...)
scheme: B1: (a) No other singer in the class is as good as he is.
B1: (b) Hardly had the guests left when we cleaned up.
long.ans: (a) No other singer in the class is as good as he is. (b) Hardly had the guests left when we cleaned up.

long.q: Rewrite as instructed: (a) It is not possible to finish the work today. (Use: impossible) (b) You must not park here. (Begin: Parking...) (c) She said, “How beautiful the sunset is!” (Report the exclamation) (d) As he was ill, he stayed at home. (Use: owing to)
scheme: B1: (a) It is impossible to finish the work today.
B1: (b) Parking is not allowed here. (or: Parking here is prohibited.)
B1: (c) She exclaimed that the sunset was very beautiful.
B1: (d) Owing to his illness, he stayed at home.

questions.q: Change to indirect speech: He said, “I am busy.”
o: He said that I am busy.
He said that he is being busy.
He said that he was busy.
questions.why: With a past reporting verb, the pronoun changes and the present tense moves back to the past.

questions.q: Change to indirect speech: She said to me, “Where do you live?”
o: She asked me where do I live.
She said me where I lived?
She asked me that where did I live.
She asked me where I lived.
questions.why: A question becomes a statement word order, with 'asked' and no question mark.

questions.q: Change to indirect speech: The teacher said, “The earth goes round the sun.”
o: The teacher said that the earth goes round the sun.
The teacher said that the earth went round the sun yesterday.
The teacher said that the earth had gone round the sun.
The teacher asked whether the earth goes round the sun.
questions.why: A universal truth keeps its present tense in reported speech.

questions.q: Change to indirect speech: “Please help me,” she said to him.
o: She said him please help her.
She requested him to help her.
She requested him that help me.
She ordered him to help me please.
questions.why: Polite commands are reported with 'requested' + object + to-infinitive.

questions.q: Change to indirect speech: He said, “I will come tomorrow.”
o: He said that he will come tomorrow.
He said that I would come the next day.
He said that he would come the next day.
He said that he would came the next day.
questions.why: 'Will' becomes 'would' and 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day' after a past reporting verb.

long.q: Change into indirect speech: (a) Rahul said, “I have lost my wallet.” (b) Mother said to me, “Did you lock the door?” (c) The captain said to the team, “Do not lose heart.”
scheme: B1: (a) Rahul said that he had lost his wallet.
B1: (b) Mother asked me if/whether I had locked the door.
B1: (c) The captain told/urged the team not to lose heart.

long.q: Change into direct speech: (a) She told me that she was going to Shillong the next week. (b) The old man asked the boy what his name was.
scheme: B1: (a) She said to me, “I am going to Shillong next week.”
B1: (b) The old man said to the boy, “What is your name?”

long.q: Report this conversation in indirect speech: Asha said to Vikram, “Can you lend me your notes?” Vikram said, “Of course, I will bring them tomorrow.”
scheme: B1: Asha asked Vikram if he could lend her his notes.
B1: Vikram agreed (or: replied that of course he would)
B1: and said that he would bring them the next day.

long.q: Change into indirect speech: (a) He said, “What a lovely garden this is!” (b) The guard said to us, “Let us wait here.”
scheme: B1: (a) He exclaimed that it was a very lovely garden.
B1: (b) The guard suggested to us that we should wait there.
long.ans: (a) He exclaimed that it was a very lovely garden. (b) The guard suggested that we should wait there.

long.q: State four changes that usually happen when a statement in the present tense is reported after a past reporting verb, and give an example.
scheme: B1: the tense moves one step back (e.g. is → was, has → had)
B1: pronouns change to fit the speaker and listener
B1: words of time and place change (now → then, here → there, today → that day)
B1: inverted commas are removed and 'that' is often added, e.g. He said, “I am here now.” → He said that he was there then.

questions.q: Change to the passive: 'The chef cooked a delicious meal.'
o: A delicious meal is cooked by the chef.
A delicious meal has cooked the chef.
The chef was cooked by a delicious meal.
A delicious meal was cooked by the chef.
questions.why: The object becomes the subject and the verb becomes 'was' + past participle, keeping the past tense.

questions.q: Change to the passive: 'They are building a new bridge over the Brahmaputra.'
o: A new bridge is being built over the Brahmaputra.
A new bridge is built over the Brahmaputra.
A new bridge was being built over the Brahmaputra.
A new bridge has built over the Brahmaputra.
questions.why: Present continuous passive uses 'is being' + past participle; 'by them' can be dropped.

questions.q: Change to the passive: 'Who wrote this letter?'
o: By whom was this letter written?
By whom this letter was written?
questions.why: 'Who' becomes 'By whom' and question word order is kept: was + subject + past participle.

questions.q: Change to the passive: 'Shut the door.'
questions.why: Commands become 'Let + object + be + past participle'.

questions.q: The passive voice is usually preferred when
o: the doer must be emphasised as the subject
the sentence is a question beginning with 'why'
the doer of the action is unknown or unimportant
questions.why: 'My bicycle has been stolen' focuses on what happened, since the thief is unknown.

long.q: Change into the passive voice: (a) The police have caught the thief. (b) The farmers will harvest the rice next week. (c) Somebody is following us. (d) People speak Tamil in Chennai.
scheme: B1: (a) The thief has been caught by the police.
B1: (b) The rice will be harvested by the farmers next week.
B1: (c) We are being followed.
B1: (d) Tamil is spoken in Chennai.

long.q: Change into the active voice: (a) The match was won by our school. (b) The parcel had been delivered before noon. (c) Let the work be done at once.
scheme: B1: (a) Our school won the match.
B1: (b) Somebody had delivered the parcel before noon.
B1: (c) Do the work at once.

long.q: Rewrite in the passive, beginning with the words given: (a) We must save water. (Water...) (b) They gave the winner a trophy. (The winner...) (c) Did your sister paint this picture? (Was...)
scheme: B1: (a) Water must be saved.
B1: (b) The winner was given a trophy.
B1: (c) Was this picture painted by your sister?

long.q: Explain why notices often use the passive voice, and rewrite this sentence in the passive: 'The Principal requests all students to wear their uniforms.'
scheme: B1: it keeps the tone formal and impersonal and focuses on the action or the readers
B1: All students are requested to wear their uniforms.

long.q: Change the voice in each: (a) The students had completed the project. (b) The bridge was being repaired when we passed. (c) Everybody loves her. (d) Close the windows.
scheme: B1: (a) The project had been completed by the students.
B1: (b) They/Workers were repairing the bridge when we passed.
B1: (c) She is loved by everybody.
B1: (d) Let the windows be closed.
